Data centers constructed for hyperscalers to lease are off-balance sheet during construction. Hyperscalers, in partnership with private credit, create Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) to finance data center developments. These SPVs are considered "variable interest entities" (VIE) for accounting purposes because as the sole tenant of the data center, hyperscalers have more exposure to and influence on the SPV than their minority equity ownership and voting rights would suggest.

VIE structures became increasingly common and used to circumvent consolidation in the late '90s and early '00s, just before the dot com bubble burst and around the time of the massive fiber overbuild. In response, consolidation accounting was updated so that VIEs would be consolidated by the SPV's "primary beneficiary". For a hyperscaler to be considered the primary beneficiary of a lease SPV, it must have both (1) the power to direct the most economically significant activities and (2) the obligation to absorb the entity's losses or the right to receive the entity's economic benefits.

Neil thinks 90% of AI workloads will run in the background versus real time.

In that future, latency matters less and cost matters more, and he's configured his company around a unique way of serving tokens at the cheapest possible price.

"There's no bad chips. There's only bad pricing, and I will make any chip work at the right price. Let's talk about AMD, great chips overall. 

People don't understand how to program them very well. That's music to my ears. I'm happy for them to sleep on this chip and for me to buy as much as I can."

"One of the ways I describe what we do is, we will buy any chip anywhere in the world for any duration of time. 

That is a level of flexibility and liquidity that no one else has right now. You'd have basically zero buyers for a data center that is ninety-five percent uptime. I'm that first buyer. 

First we scavenge chips, and then we scavenge power for those chips. 

The idea is, in both cases, I do not want to be bidding against Anthropic or OpenAI for compute capacity. I'm not gonna win against them, and I don't want to. 

I want to be more creative and use the supply that they don't find legible today. 

Over time I amass enough aggregate supply...and build my aggregate factory that is unbeatable in economics."

"My whole goal is to so dramatically expand the supply of power across the United States that I have a home for a lot of chips that otherwise would not have earned their place in a data center."

"We've really pushed AI to be an interactive chatbot tool, and everyone has chosen latency optimization because the shape of usage was chatbot oriented. 

That's the most profound change we're going to see in the next year, we're gonna move away from chatbots to more proactive or background agents, and in that world, it makes a lot more sense to build a stack around throughput."

"I love this market because it's unbounded. There's no human in the loop, so you can consume as many tokens as you like in the background versus human attention span. 

So long term, we're going to end this year at maybe fifty-fifty background and real time workloads, but I see this going to ninety ten in favor of background."

"The best latency is no latency at all. When you wake up in the morning, the work's already been done overnight, you didn't even have to ask for it. 

What we'd like is the agent to operate on more human time scales. You don't manage your colleagues every five minutes. You come back and check in maybe once a week."

"My job is to make the tokens as cheap as humanly possible, and I will do it through every layer in the stack available to me."

A good example comes from a 16th-century English village. A farming household might include not only parents and their children, but several unrelated teenagers or young adults. They were called “servants,” who were the children of other farming families who had temporarily left their own homes to work for wages. A farmer’s 16-year-old son or daughter, for example, might leave their parents, move several villages away, and spend a few years working in another household. They each would later marry and establish households of their own. Historians such as Peter Laslett and Richard Wall refer to this period between leaving the parental household and marriage as “life-cycle service.”
This created a distinct period between childhood and marriage. By his early 20s, a young Englishman might already have spent years earning wages, living among strangers, going on adventures, changing employers, and moving between communities and villages. Independence (in the modern sense) was, therefore, experienced well before the formation of a family of one’s own.

Investors are moving away from long-term bonds.

Treasury Bill ETFs have attracted +$51 billion in inflows since February 27th, the most among all fixed-income categories.

Over the same period, ETFs tracking long-term bonds have attracted just +$7 billion.

This is despite long-term bonds offering a higher ~4.7% indicated yield versus the ~3.7% for Treasury Bill ETFs.

However, long-term bonds can lose significant value when yields rise, while Treasury Bills are much less sensitive to changes in yields.

This risk has become increasingly important, with the 30Y Treasury yield rising +70 basis points since February 27th, now at 2007 levels.

Investors are choosing lower yields in exchange for lower risk.

when it gets approved, ANY community can use glyph for shopify checkout

but today we used tokenproof and it’ll probably be the last time we do that

All right back to $SMTC movie: "The bottleneck go Brrr":

My favorite quote was: "availability currently matters more than pricing". 

In the current market for optical products. 

- No near-term erosion is expected on booked optical orders, which signals they're passing cost increases through fine.

- I was actually curious most about Semtec's CW laser products after the HieFo takeover:

Semtech expects CW-laser revenue for transceivers to begin H1 FY28. Explicitly said capacity is limited.

They still seem materially further behind compared to the laser leaders, but they're making progress for 2027 ramp. 

- TIA and driver solutions remain in exceptionally strong demand (confirmed from $AAOI earnings). 

Continues to deepen engagement across all the leading hyperscalers.  

"We are now designing to every module provider", expected 50%+ market share for 1.6T FiberEdge (TIA + driver) by years end. 

Very strong statement to make about being majority market share. 

- 1.6T FiberEdge qualifications finishing earlier than expected (good read through for your pluggable makers eg. AOI)

q: "quick thoughts on how long into 2028 does that backlog extend?"

a: The backlog for the remaining of this fiscal year, I would say for our  target is all booked. For the next year, we probably over 70% there.

Management said current capacity may not be enough for fiscal 2028, especially in the second half (great demand visibility)

Q2 revenue: 
- $341.9M vs. ~$329M expected
- adjusted EPS was $0.71 vs. $0.61

Q3 guidance was most exciting:
$410M revenue vs. ~$360M revenue
$1.05 EPS vs. $0.73 EPS. 

yeah... just look at that beautiful revenue inflection Q/Q. 

So gigantic beat, great read through on 1.6T ramp. I don't own Semtec, but these were amazing earnings.

The safest layer of corporate debt is not as safe as it used to be.

When a loan defaults now, first-lien lenders recover 61 cents on the dollar, down from 77 last cycle. Unsecured is worse: 9 cents, down from 29. Out-of-court restructurings keep reshuffling who gets paid without cutting debt, and asset-light software borrowers leave almost nothing to seize.

Private credit and leveraged-loan funds are selling "senior secured" to retirement savers on the old math. When defaults climb, the losses land harder than the models assume.

Shout out to the Coinbase listing team.

For years now I’ve been sharing horror stories about CEXs that I’ve picked up from founders, other investors and industry insiders, about how shady exchanges and their listing teams enrich themselves at the expense of both founders and their own user base through listings.

Turns out it didn’t fall on deaf ears. 

The Coinbase listing team themselves reached out to me, because they saw my criticism, appreciate it, and are always open to feedback on how they can keep improving their listing processes.

Had an extensive call with them about it, and while it wasn’t particularly surprising, the Coinbase listing team is probably one of the very few that is genuinely trustable and compliant. They don’t try to squeeze founders, they simply list the best assets that people actually want, and they genuinely care about the industry for the long term.

I found it really impressive how transparent they were, walking me through everything from front to back, sharing how their listing processes work and how they try to strike the right balance between memecoin listings and fundamentally strong projects.

And even more impressive was how genuinely interested they were in my takes on what could still be improved in the listing process, what I’d like to see, and how they can ultimately become an even better exchange. They genuinely care and listen.

Really like how they’re approaching listings, for two reasons:

1) they are truly 100% free. And I mean 100% free, no hidden costs like airdrop budgets or range rovers that come attached.

2) while volume should be their main focus and KPI as a business, they try to optimize for what’s best for their user base and this industry overall.

Much smarter and more long term oriented than many of the other shady CEXs that just try to extract as much as possible in the moment.

It goes to show once again why Coinbase is the oldest and most trustable exchange out there. 

They’ve always played the honest, long term game, and it has paid off big time so far. I don’t expect it to be any different this time.

After all, here’s what makes me happiest about all of this:

Massive confirmation that it’s worth speaking up, and that we don’t always have to just accept everything and swallow it.

It might not be much, but I’m proud to be contributing to a better industry, and I’ll keep doing so.

You can do it too.

☢️ AN OIL SUPERPOWER WANTS A NUCLEAR FLEET.

The proposed U.S.–Saudi civil-nuclear agreement has now been sent to Congress.

If it advances, the 30-year pact could pave the way for Westinghouse AP1000 reactors in Saudi Arabia—a project potentially worth tens of billions of dollars.

This would be much more than a reactor-construction contract. A Saudi fleet would create recurring demand across the entire nuclear fuel cycle:

• Uranium
• Conversion
• Enrichment
• Fuel fabrication

Westinghouse is jointly owned by Cameco $CCJ and Brookfield. Every new reactor is not a one-off uranium purchase—it becomes a fuel customer for decades.

Political hurdles remain. Congress has 90 session days to review the pact, non-proliferation concerns will be contentious, and President Trump says implementation depends on Saudi Arabia normalizing relations with Israel.

The deal is therefore far from guaranteed.

But zoom out.

Saudi Arabia—an oil superpower—is pursuing nuclear power as part of its future energy system. If Riyadh builds an AP1000 fleet, the uranium market gains an entirely new source of long-term demand while utilities are already competing to secure future supply.

The uranium bull case is no longer built only on reactor restarts and life extensions.

It is increasingly being built on new countries, new fleets and new decades of fuel demand.

The political route remains conditional.

Saudi Arabia’s nuclear ambition does not.

⚡ THE DAILY METALS PULSE — 26 AUGUST 2026 ⚡

Four metals. One pulse. No noise.

The Asian session has delivered a split macro signal.

Brent crude fell for a third consecutive session, dropping more than 2% to around $86.41/bbl as markets priced in hopes that renewed Iran–Oman talks could eventually help reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

That pushed the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield down to approximately 4.63%, while the Dollar Index remained just below 99 at around 98.93.

But the inflation warning has not disappeared.

Australian CPI rose 1.0% MoM in July, while core inflation remained at 3.6%. Markets more than doubled the probability of a September RBA rate hike from 17% to 36%.

Japan’s corporate-services inflation also accelerated from 3.4% to 3.6%, strengthening expectations that the Bank of Japan could hike in September.

Near-term energy pressure is easing. Underlying inflation remains sticky.

☢️ URANIUM — A new potential demand catalyst emerged overnight as the Trump administration sent a 30-year civil-nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia to Congress.

If implemented, the agreement could enable the construction of Westinghouse AP1000 reactors worth tens of billions of dollars—eventually creating additional uranium demand. However, the pact remains conditional on Saudi Arabia normalizing relations with Israel, so this is potential rather than bankable demand.

🟠 COPPER — Front-month COMEX copper recorded its highest-ever close at approximately $6.71/lb and remained near $6.72 during Asian trading.

Copper is holding firm despite cautious Asian equities and yesterday’s weaker U.S. consumer data. The tariff-driven geographic supply imbalance continues to outweigh conventional cyclical concerns.

🥈 SILVER — Silver gained approximately 0.9% to $69.26/oz, clearly outperforming gold and bringing the gold–silver ratio down to around 67.

With Treasury yields falling, silver’s monetary side is receiving support while the metal again approaches the psychologically important $70 level.

🥇 GOLD — Gold eased approximately 0.3% to $4,643/oz but remains close to Tuesday’s three-month high.

Lower oil and bond yields are supportive, but traders are reluctant to chase the move before today’s U.S. PCE inflation report at 12:30 GMT.

BTC's getting close to $80K and the price targets are already flying.

Well, the main thing I'm watching is who's doing the buying.

The move started like a classic squeeze. Short liquidation levels were stacked right above BTC, and buyers came in hard around the mid-$60Ks. Once price pushed into those levels, the forced buying did the rest.

That's the part that makes me nervous. When the long side gets this crowded and levered, one bad headline is all it takes to kick off a liquidation cascade.

The early bull signs are real.

• ETF inflows holding near that $3B weekly pace instead of fading
• Funding and the futures premium cooling off while price holds
• Breadth staying above 80% through the first real pullback

Be smart about it. No chasing, and no leverage. The recovery looks real to me, and so does the cascade risk. 

There’s going to be flush imo. You wanna be the one who buys and benefits from it than the guy getting liquidated.

thread_tweets.text:
1: Onboarding & “What do I actually do after first launch?”

> Pick one recommended model.
> Ignore ALL advanced settings for now.
> Open a normal Hermes session.
> Give it one real task you already need done.
> Try 2–3 example workflows.
> Connect Discord/Telegram only if you want remote access.
> Add scheduled jobs only after the basic agent works.
> Learn profiles, bots and orchestration later.

You will want to run before you can walk, so make sure you just nail the basics.

We’ll get on to the rest of it all shortly.

thread_tweets.text:
2: Profiles, Bots, Orchestration & Subagents

> Start with one main profile.
> Use that profile for general work.
> Create a new profile only when you need different instructions, memory or a different model.
> Give each specialist one clear job, such as research, coding or writing.
> Tell the main agent exactly when to use each specialist.
> Tell it: “Delegate research tasks to the Research profile.”
> Specify the model and effort level when creating a specialist.
> Keep shared project information in the project/workspace, not inside one agent.
> Test delegation with one simple task before building a large multi-agent setup.
> Only add agent-to-agent communication once the individual agents work properly.

3: Remote Access, Gateways & Multi-device

> Decide where Hermes will run: your computer or a server.
> Use local mode if you only need Hermes while that computer is on.
> Use a VPS/server if you want Hermes available 24/7.
> Run the Hermes gateway on the machine hosting the agent.
> Create the gateway/API credentials.
> Connect your laptop Desktop app to that gateway.
> Use Tailscale if the server is not publicly accessible.
> Test one remote chat before setting up anything else.
> Connect Telegram/Discord if you also want phone access.
> Keep one main gateway where possible instead of creating separate setups for every device.

5: Memory, Skills & Structure

> Do not put everything into memory.
> Save only facts Hermes will need again.
> Keep permanent preferences in memory.
> Put repeatable procedures into Skills instead.
> Create one Skill for each repeated workflow.
> Give Skills clear names such as “Research Leads” or “Clean Inbox”.
> Install new Skills only when you actually need them.
> Remove or disable tools and Skills you never use.
> Review memory occasionally and delete outdated information.
> Treat memory like organised reference material, not a running diary.

WHO PAYS FOR THE DAM WATER?

Everyone is throwing around numbers on data center water use vs. golf courses, so we went back to the sources.

Golf: 1.63M acre-ft, or 531B gallons (GCSAA, 2024)
Data centers: 17.4B gallons direct, 211B gallons indirect (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, 2023)

So golf uses 30x more water than data centers at the site: 531B vs. 17.4B.

Add the water attributed to generating the necessary electricity and the gap collapses to 2.3x: 531B vs. 228B.

How to treat hydropower in this equation is where things get very weird -->

LBNL counts evaporation from hydro reservoirs as water consumed generating electricity. Fair enough. But reservoirs often serve several purposes, so you have to decide how much of that evaporation actually belongs to power.

The methodology uses a surprisingly binary rule. If hydropower is listed as a reservoir's primary purpose in the federal National Inventory of Dams, electricity gets charged 100% of the evaporation. If hydro is secondary, it gets zero.

This matters a lot: Hydro supplies only ~5.5% of U.S. electricity, but reservoir evaporation accounts for roughly 60% of the water LBNL attributes to data centers' electricity use.

Libby Dam in Montana is a good example of how strange this can get.

The federal database lists its primary purpose as hydropower, so electricity gets charged with 100% of Lake Koocanusa's evaporation.

But the Army Corps operates Libby for flood-risk management and hydropower, along with recreation, fish and wildlife and water quality. Nearly 5 million acre-ft of the reservoir is allocated to flood storage.

Grand Coulee shows the problem in reverse. It's the largest hydropower complex in the U.S. and can generate ~21 TWh a year. But the federal database lists its primary purpose as flood-risk reduction, so its reservoir evaporation isn't charged to hydropower at all. It also irrigates ~680,000 acres.

There isn't one obvious answer here. But that's the problem with a 100-or-zero rule for multipurpose reservoirs. A huge amount of water can move on or off electricity's tab based on which purpose occupies one field in a federal database.

Use USGS/NLR power-sector estimates that exclude hydro evaporation and indirect data center water use falls from 211B gallons to roughly 83B.

Suddenly golf isn't using 2.3x as much water as data centers. It's closer to 5x.

Now, looking forward:

Golf water use is down 31% since 2005 and another 3.2% since 2020. Data center power demand obviously isn't down. LBNL now estimates 649 TWh of annual electricity consumption in 2030, equivalent to ~74 GW running continuously, versus ~20 GW in 2023.

Direct data center water use was only 17.4B gallons in 2023. Even if water intensity doesn't improve at all, 3.7x the power demand gets you to ~64B gallons in 2030. Golf is at 531B today.

And the direct data center estimate is almost certainly too high. More than half of new hyperscale builds are moving to closed-loop cooling (90%+ less water use), so direct water use should grow much more slowly than power demand.

For a deliberately conservative comparison, though, assume no improvement at all. Scale today's entire direct + electricity footprint with demand, but leave out hydro reservoir evaporation, and you get roughly 370B gallons in 2030.

Still ~30% below golf.

(Count hydro evaporation, though, and data centers pass golf before 2030.

Turns out the delta mostly comes down to who pays for the dam water.)
